# California Proposition 99

**Source**: the `smoking` dataset in the `edunford/tidysynth` R package (MIT licence, Eric Dunford,
https://github.com/edunford/tidysynth), which distributes Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller's
Proposition 99 panel — the classic worked example for synthetic control, from Abadie, Diamond &
Hainmueller (2010, JASA), following the method introduced in Abadie & Gardeazabal (2003). Fetched as
`data/smoking.rda` (17,505 bytes) and converted to CSV with `pyreadr` on 2026-09-04, content
unchanged except for one added `treatment` column, `year` cast from float to int, and a sort by
`(state, year)`.

**Rows**: 1,209 — a balanced panel of 39 states × 31 years, 1970–2000.

**Columns**: `state`, `year`, `cigsale` (cigarette sales, packs per capita), `lnincome` (log mean
income), `beer` (beer consumption per capita), `age15to24` (proportion of the population aged
15–24), `retprice` (retail price of a pack of cigarettes), `treatment` (added: 1 for California from
1989 onward, 0 otherwise).

**Treatment**: `treatment`. **Outcome**: `cigsale`. **Unit**: `state`. **Time**: `year`.

`treatment` is not present in the original data and encodes a choice: Proposition 99 passed in
November 1988, and 1989 is its first full year of effect and Abadie et al.'s own first
post-treatment year. That gives California 12 treated rows (1989–2000) out of its 31.

**The intended causal question**: did Proposition 99, California's 1988 tobacco-control law, reduce
cigarette consumption relative to a synthetic counterfactual built from the other 38 states?
California's own series falls from 123.0 packs per capita in 1970 to 90.1 in 1988, the last
pre-treatment year, and on to 41.6 by 2000 — but so does the national trend, which is exactly why
a counterfactual is needed rather than a before-and-after comparison. Abadie et al.'s published
result is the external benchmark this project's own `SyntheticControl` implementation is scored
against, and it is genuine validation of this codebase: unlike every simulated scenario, nothing
here was generated by code this project also wrote.

**Missing values are structural, and whole-year**: three predictor columns are absent for entire
years across all 39 states at once, rather than scattered per state.

| column | present for | missing for |
|---|---|---|
| `lnincome` | 1972–1997 (26 years) | 1970–1971, 1998–2000 |
| `beer` | 1984–1997 (14 years) | 1970–1983, 1998–2000 |
| `age15to24` | 1970–1990 (21 years) | 1991–2000 |

`cigsale`, `retprice`, `state` and `year` are complete. This matches the original dataset and is not
an artefact of the conversion. It is also why Abadie et al. average their predictors over specific
year windows rather than uniformly over the whole panel — no single window has all three available.
This project's `SyntheticControl` uses the pre-treatment outcome path itself rather than these
predictors, so it reads only complete columns; anything that later wants `beer` or `lnincome` must
choose a window first.

**Known limitations**: no causal claims beyond what Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller's published
analysis already established are made from this fixture. The 39 states are the donor pool that paper
retained after excluding states that adopted their own large tobacco-control programmes; the
exclusion decisions are inherited from the source, not made here.
